Root Uptake of Sub-Micron Plastic Particles and Trophic Transfer to Crops

Author: Prof. Kenji Takahashi | November 20, 2025 | Experimental Botany

Apoplastic Entry and Vascular Translocation

While microplastics exceeding 5 micrometers are mechanically prevented from crossing intact root epidermis barriers, sub-micron and nanoscale plastic particles (sub-100 nm) exhibit significant bioavailability to vascular plants. Utilizing fluorescent polystyrene beads and confocal laser scanning microscopy, our investigations tracked the cellular translocation of 40-nm nanoplastics in hydroponically grown and soil-potted wheat (Triticum aestivum) and lettuce (Lactuca sativa).

Nanoplastics penetrate root tips through crack-entry sites formed during lateral root emergence. Once entering the root stele, the nanoparticles enter xylem vessels and are pulled upward via transpirational pull, accumulating in stem parenchyma and foliar leaf tissues at concentrations up to 4.8 micrograms per gram of dry shoot biomass.

Bioaccumulation Across Invertebrate Trophic Levels

Feeding assays with herbivorous agricultural pests (aphids and snails) consuming contaminated crop foliage demonstrated secondary trophic bioaccumulation factors of 1.4 to 2.1. These findings establish that nanoscale plastics in agricultural soils effectively breach biological barriers and enter human-consumed food chains.
